➔ Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is a cytosol enzyme, ​more specific to the liver​,\nso that a rise only ​occurs with liver disease​.
Liver function tests: Aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT or SGOT) and alanine aminotransferase (ALAT or SGPT) levels are elevated in hepatocellular disease.
As a reflection of cytopathic injury to the hepatocytes, there is a rise in serum levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST).
AST (Aspartate aminotransferase) and ALT (Alanine aminotransferase) are intracellular enzymes.

Examples include Acid Phosphatase, found in the prostate gland, liver, spleen, and RBCs; Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT), which is primarily specific to the liver; and Amylase and Lipase, which are highly specific to the pancreas.
Pyruvate + Glutamate ⇌ Alanine + α‑Ketoglutarate (catalysed by alanine aminotransferase).

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman is evaluated for acute epigastric pain and vomiting following a fatty meal. Laboratory studies show an elevated alanine aminotransferase and lipase. What is the primary initiating factor in this patient's condition?
o: Direct toxic destruction of acinar cell mitochondrial membranes
Autoimmune-mediated destruction of the ampulla of Vater
Transient or persistent obstruction of the pancreatic duct
Bacterial translocation from the biliary tree into the pancreas
qs.e: Gallstones passing through the choledochoduodenal junction cause transient or persistent obstruction of the pancreatic duct, raising hydrostatic pressure. This differs from alcoholic pancreatitis, which involves direct toxin-induced acinar cell injury.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: ALT is an intracellular enzyme that transfers an amino group from alanine to α‑ketoglutarate, producing pyruvate. It is released into the blood when hepatocytes are damaged, making it a sensitive marker of liver injury.

sections.p: ALT (alanine aminotransferase) is a cytosolic enzyme mainly in the liver. Its serum level rises when hepatocytes are injured, reflecting hepatocellular damage.
b: High ALT = liver cell injury; normal ALT = no significant hepatocellular damage

sections.p: ALT catalyses the reversible transamination of alanine and α‑ketoglutarate to pyruvate and glutamate. The reaction is part of gluconeogenesis and amino‑acid metabolism.
ALT activity is regulated by substrate availability and cellular energy status. It is not tightly regulated by feedback; its serum level reflects cell membrane integrity.
Any condition that injures hepatocytes releases ALT into the bloodstream. Causes are grouped by mechanism: toxic, viral, metabolic, ischemic, or autoimmune.
ALT is the most specific serum marker for hepatocellular injury. It guides diagnosis, monitors disease activity, and assesses treatment response.
b: ALT 1–3× ULN may indicate chronic disease

t.b: High ALT indicates acute injury; moderate elevation suggests chronic disease
Ultrasound detects steatosis, cirrhosis, or tumors

sections.p: Remember that ALT is more liver‑specific than AST. In low‑resource settings, a single ALT measurement can triage patients for further testing.
b: ALT is the preferred test for hepatocellular injury
AST/ALT ratio helps distinguish alcohol from viral causes

whenToSeekHelp: Severe jaundice, confusion, abdominal pain, or sudden rise in ALT >10× ULN
Signs of acute liver failure such as coagulopathy or encephalopathy

faq.q: Why is ALT more specific to the liver than AST?
faq.a: AST is found in heart, muscle, kidney, and brain, so its elevation can reflect injury elsewhere. ALT is largely confined to hepatocytes.

faq.q: Can ALT be normal in liver disease?
faq.a: Yes, especially in early chronic hepatitis or in patients with fatty liver; ALT can be normal while fibrosis progresses.

faq.q: What does an AST/ALT ratio >2 indicate?
faq.a: It suggests alcoholic liver disease; in viral hepatitis the ratio is usually <1.
